explain.title: How it works
explain.example: Illustrative flow · not live model values
explain.reduced: Reduced motion: use the step controls to explore.
explain.cnn.summary: Finds local patterns in content and pools them into one item vector.
explain.cnn.use: Use for local phrases or short content patterns.
explain.cnn.difference: CNN pools all configured fields together; CNNCat pools each field separately, then concatenates.
explain.cnn.step.0.title: Read token features
explain.cnn.step.0.body: Five input circles represent five title tokens. Hover to read the feature values.
explain.cnn.step.1.title: Apply a shared kernel
explain.cnn.step.1.body: c1, c2, and c3 each receive three neighboring tokens with shared weights [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]. Inspect the weighted sum, bias, and ReLU.
explain.cnn.step.2.title: Attend and aggregate
explain.cnn.step.2.body: Local responses pass through tanh scoring and softmax to obtain α. Weighted products are summed; attention weights are computed from upstream values.
explain.cnn.step.3.title: Read the item feature
explain.cnn.step.3.body: The green node outputs the pooled response. Trace its contributors along the connections. A full encoder can have many channels.
explain.cnncat.summary: Encodes content fields separately and concatenates their vectors.
explain.cnncat.use: Use when field-specific representations should remain separate in the output.
explain.cnncat.difference: Its output dimension grows with the number of fields; it does not pool all fields into one fixed-width vector.
explain.cnncat.step.0.title: Read title and category
explain.cnncat.step.0.body: The title uses one feature channel across five tokens; category is an already encoded two-dimensional category feature.
explain.cnncat.step.1.title: Convolve local patterns
explain.cnncat.step.1.body: Three neighboring title tokens feed each ReLU convolution neuron; all three positions share the kernel.
explain.cnncat.step.2.title: Keep field-specific features
explain.cnncat.step.2.body: The title is pooled separately using additive attention; the category retains its own values.
explain.cnncat.step.3.title: Concatenate outputs
explain.cnncat.step.3.body: Three green nodes show the title result and two category dimensions. Concatenation arranges dimensions without adding them.
explain.ada.summary: Learns which sequence positions matter and combines them into one vector.
explain.ada.use: Use for a lightweight learned summary of tokens or clicked items.
explain.ada.difference: Unlike self-attention, it pools existing vectors without first exchanging information between positions.
explain.ada.step.0.title: Expand input vectors
explain.ada.step.0.body: Each x contains two dimensions, each drawn as a circle. Inputs may represent tokens, fields, or history items.
explain.ada.step.1.title: Learn importance
explain.ada.step.1.body: Each input passes through a biased tanh neuron and a scoring layer, followed by shared softmax. Hover over α to inspect every score in its denominator.
explain.ada.step.2.title: Sum weighted dimensions
explain.ada.step.2.body: Each feature dimension is multiplied by its input’s α, then summed with the same dimension from other inputs.
explain.ada.step.3.title: Output one vector
explain.ada.step.3.body: The green outputs retain two dimensions. Attention weights are computed contributions, rather than fixed constants.
explain.attention.summary: Exchanges information across a sequence using multiple attention heads, then pools it.
explain.attention.use: Use to learn relationships between content tokens or historical interests.
explain.attention.difference: This operator uses one multi-head attention module plus additive pooling; Transformer stacks full encoder blocks.
explain.attention.step.0.title: Read two positions
explain.attention.step.0.body: Two two-dimensional inputs represent reading events or tokens; each dimension is a separate circle.
explain.attention.step.1.title: Attend with two heads
explain.attention.step.1.body: Each head generates Q, K, and V, then QK scores, softmax, and weighted V. Each head has one dimension, so the scale is √1.
explain.attention.step.2.title: Merge and pool
explain.attention.step.2.body: Heads project back to two dimensions. Additive attention then pools positions; inspect the distinct head and pooling weights.
explain.attention.step.3.title: Read contextual output
explain.attention.step.3.body: Green nodes output the pooled contextual feature. Each input can influence another position through attention.
explain.gru.summary: Reads the sequence in order and compresses it into a final state.
explain.gru.use: Use when sequence order should affect the representation.
explain.gru.difference: Unlike pooling, GRU updates a hidden state recurrently. This implementation projects the last layer’s final state.
explain.gru.step.0.title: Read ordered history
explain.gru.step.0.body: Inputs include three reading events and initial state h0. Reverse the order to compare the same events in a different sequence.
explain.gru.step.1.title: Update recurrent state
explain.gru.step.1.body: r controls old information in the candidate state; z interpolates between the new candidate and old state. Inspect gates, products, and h nodes to follow recurrence.
explain.gru.step.2.title: Project the final state
explain.gru.step.2.body: The last h passes through a linear projection into the output dimensions. Inspect its connection weights.
explain.gru.step.3.title: Compare order effects
explain.gru.step.3.body: Green nodes show the result. Switching original / reverse order recomputes the recurrent network.
explain.pooling.summary: Summarizes a sequence using mean or max pooling.
explain.pooling.use: Use as a simple baseline or to aggregate existing representations.
explain.pooling.difference: No learned attention weights or recurrent state. The max_pooling and flatten settings change aggregation.
explain.pooling.step.0.title: Read features and masks
explain.pooling.step.0.body: Three two-dimensional inputs have validity masks; all are 1 in this example.
explain.pooling.step.1.title: Keep valid positions
explain.pooling.step.1.body: Each dimension is multiplied by its mask. Gray nodes represent parameter-free operations.
explain.pooling.step.2.title: Aggregate by dimension
explain.pooling.step.2.body: Mean pooling sums and divides by the valid count; max pooling selects each dimension’s largest value. Switch rules with the buttons.
explain.pooling.step.3.title: Output fixed dimensions
explain.pooling.step.3.body: The output retains two dimensions regardless of sequence length. Inspect the sources of each mean or maximum.
explain.transformer.summary: Uses Transformer layers to encode a sequence and return a summary.
explain.transformer.use: Use for context-dependent relationships within the sequence.
explain.transformer.difference: This is a configurable BERT-style encoder, distinct from loading a pretrained BERT checkpoint.
explain.transformer.step.0.title: Prepare two positions
explain.transformer.step.0.body: Each position becomes two input nodes; the network expands left to right by dependency.
explain.transformer.step.1.title: Expand one encoder block
explain.transformer.step.1.body: Two-head Q/K/V attention is followed by residual and layer normalization, a GELU feed-forward layer, and another residual normalization.
explain.transformer.step.2.title: Project and attention-pool
explain.transformer.step.2.body: Projected positions pass through tanh scoring and softmax before a dimensionwise weighted sum.
explain.transformer.step.3.title: Read the encoded result
explain.transformer.step.3.body: Inspect green nodes for the final computation, then trace left through normalization and attention nodes.
explain.fastformer.summary: Uses Fastformer layers to encode a sequence and return a summary.
explain.fastformer.use: Use for context-dependent relationships within the sequence.
explain.fastformer.difference: Fastformer uses global query/key summaries rather than a full pairwise attention matrix.
explain.fastformer.step.0.title: Prepare position features
explain.fastformer.step.0.body: Two positions each have two dimensions, keeping the global attention calculation inspectable.
explain.fastformer.step.1.title: Aggregate a global query
explain.fastformer.step.1.body: Project Q and K, then score, normalize, and sum Q to obtain global q̄.
explain.fastformer.step.2.title: Modulate content with a global key
explain.fastformer.step.2.body: Multiply q̄ elementwise with K, compute global k̄, and use it to modulate content; then add residuals and pool.
explain.fastformer.step.3.title: Read the pooled output
explain.fastformer.step.3.body: Green nodes show the output projection. Trace how global features influence positions.
explain.flattentransformer.summary: Uses Transformer layers to encode a flattened content sequence from user history.
explain.flattentransformer.use: Use for token-level interactions across historical items.
explain.flattentransformer.difference: This is a configurable BERT-style encoder, distinct from loading a pretrained BERT checkpoint.
explain.flattentransformer.step.0.title: Read flattened token features
explain.flattentransformer.step.0.body: Positions are tokens flattened across reading history; the core block is a Transformer.
explain.flattentransformer.step.1.title: Expand one encoder block
explain.flattentransformer.step.1.body: Two-head Q/K/V attention is followed by residual and layer normalization, a GELU feed-forward layer, and another residual normalization.
explain.flattentransformer.step.2.title: Project and attention-pool
explain.flattentransformer.step.2.body: Projected positions pass through tanh scoring and softmax before a dimensionwise weighted sum.
explain.flattentransformer.step.3.title: Read the encoded result
explain.flattentransformer.step.3.body: Inspect green nodes for the final computation, then trace left through normalization and attention nodes.
explain.flattenfastformer.summary: Uses Fastformer layers to encode a flattened content sequence from user history.
explain.flattenfastformer.use: Use for token-level interactions across historical items.
explain.flattenfastformer.difference: Fastformer uses global query/key summaries rather than a full pairwise attention matrix.
explain.flattenfastformer.step.0.title: Read flattened token features
explain.flattenfastformer.step.0.body: Positions are tokens flattened across reading history; the global attention core is Fastformer.
explain.flattenfastformer.step.1.title: Aggregate a global query
explain.flattenfastformer.step.1.body: Project Q and K, then score, normalize, and sum Q to obtain global q̄.
explain.flattenfastformer.step.2.title: Modulate content with a global key
explain.flattenfastformer.step.2.body: Multiply q̄ elementwise with K, compute global k̄, and use it to modulate content; then add residuals and pool.
explain.flattenfastformer.step.3.title: Read the pooled output
explain.flattenfastformer.step.3.body: Green nodes show the output projection. Trace how global features influence positions.
explain.polyattention.summary: Represents a user with several interest vectors instead of one.
explain.polyattention.use: Use with a compatible multi-interest predictor such as MINER.
explain.polyattention.difference: The number of context codes controls the number of interest vectors; the output remains a set of vectors.
explain.polyattention.step.0.title: Read multiple history items
explain.polyattention.step.0.body: Three two-dimensional history features participate in both interest branches.
explain.polyattention.step.1.title: Attend for each interest
explain.polyattention.step.1.body: After tanh projection, two context codes score history separately. Each branch has its own softmax distribution.
explain.polyattention.step.2.title: Form separate interest vectors
explain.polyattention.step.2.body: Each branch uses its own α to weight the original history. Inspect weighted nodes to see individual contributions.
explain.polyattention.step.3.title: Keep multiple interests
explain.polyattention.step.3.body: Four green nodes represent two two-dimensional interest vectors, retained separately.

explain.nullsimple.step.0.title: Retain original features
explain.nullsimple.step.0.body: History or prepared token sequences are expanded into two-dimensional inputs; each circle is one original value.
explain.nullsimple.step.1.title: Pass values through unchanged
explain.nullsimple.step.1.body: Copy nodes use weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trained layers.
explain.nullsimple.step.2.title: Arrange for downstream use
explain.nullsimple.step.2.body: This step represents dimension arrangement with values unchanged; variants differ in input granularity and downstream structure.
explain.nullsimple.step.3.title: Output retained features
explain.nullsimple.step.3.body: Green circles retain each dimension. Null branches also retain masks; no pooling or attention is performed.

explain.scflatten.step.1.body: Copy nodes use weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trained layers.

explain.lm.summary: Uses pretrained language-model representations to encode item content.
explain.lm.use: Use when pretrained text semantics are useful and model resources are available.
explain.lm.difference: The checkpoint family and size differ by component. Cache and fine-tuning behavior follow its parameters.
explain.lm.step.0.title: Keep the word, change its context
explain.lm.step.0.body: token1 is “chip” and token2 is context. The original token1 vector remains the same across contexts.
explain.lm.step.1.title: Inspect an attention sublayer
explain.lm.step.1.body: Inspect reduced Q/K/V and softmax calculations. Bidirectional models attend to all positions; causal models connect only to current and earlier positions.
explain.lm.step.2.title: Aggregate contextual features
explain.lm.step.2.body: Project the sublayer outputs and attention-pool them. This illustrates a core sublayer without loading the full pretrained network.
explain.lm.step.3.title: Compare contexts
explain.lm.step.3.body: Change context and observe output and intermediate values. Every node’s inspector uses the current inputs.
explain.iisan.summary: Fuses cached representations from several language-model layers with trainable side networks.
explain.iisan.use: Use to adapt pretrained semantics without repeatedly running the full backbone during recommendation training.
explain.iisan.difference: Unlike ordinary LM encoding, IISAN reads selected cached layer states and learns gated fusion through SAN blocks.
explain.iisan.step.0.title: Read cached layers
explain.iisan.step.0.body: Start with token features from three cached layers, mean-pooled per layer. The frozen language model is not rerun.
explain.iisan.step.1.title: Fuse with a learned gate
explain.iisan.step.1.body: Sigmoid converts gateLogit to μ; multiply the old state by μ and the next layer by 1−μ, then add.
explain.iisan.step.2.title: Apply SAN and continue fusion
explain.iisan.step.2.body: Up-projection, ReLU, down-projection, residual, and layer normalization form a small SAN. Fuse the next layer and project the output.
explain.iisan.step.3.title: Read adapted output
explain.iisan.step.3.body: Green nodes hold adapted item features. Inspect the separate contributions of layer fusion, SAN, and projection.
explain.externalhf.summary: Imports a Hugging Face model and pools its contextual states or pretrained token embeddings.
explain.externalhf.use: Use to bring a compatible external text checkpoint into the item encoder.
explain.externalhf.difference: Contextual mode runs the backbone; token-embeddings mode bypasses it. Both use masked mean pooling.
explain.externalhf.step.0.title: Read external token features
explain.externalhf.step.0.body: Two-dimensional inputs represent the same word in two contexts. Switch between contextual encoding and token embeddings only.
explain.externalhf.step.1.title: Compare encoding paths
explain.externalhf.step.1.body: Contextual mode expands a reduced attention sublayer. Token-only mode shows lookup outputs as copy nodes, with no contextual interaction.
explain.externalhf.step.2.title: Pool and project
explain.externalhf.step.2.body: Mean-pool token representations by dimension, then linearly project. This example’s pooling does not use attention weights.
explain.externalhf.step.3.title: Read external encoding output
explain.externalhf.step.3.body: Green nodes output item features. Mode and context changes update all inspector formulas and values.
explain.dot.summary: Multiply corresponding dimensions and sum them.
explain.dot.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.dot.difference: A lightweight matching baseline; no learned interaction network.
explain.dot.step.0.title: Expand user and candidate
explain.dot.step.0.body: u and v each have two dimensions. Changing the candidate keeps the user vector fixed.
explain.dot.step.1.title: Multiply matching dimensions
explain.dot.step.1.body: Two gray product nodes compute u[1]×v[1] and u[2]×v[2].
explain.dot.step.2.title: Sum the products
explain.dot.step.2.body: A sum node adds both products. Inspect each dimension’s contribution to the score.
explain.dot.step.3.title: Compare raw scores
explain.dot.step.3.body: The green output is a raw relevance score, without sigmoid; it is not a click probability.
explain.dnn.summary: Concatenate user and item vectors and feed them through an MLP.
explain.dnn.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.dnn.difference: Learns implicit nonlinear interactions rather than explicit cross terms.
explain.dnn.step.0.title: Concatenate input features
explain.dnn.step.0.body: Four scalar dimensions from u and v enter the network together. Inspect the concrete input values.
explain.dnn.step.1.title: Activate hidden neurons
explain.dnn.step.1.body: Two ReLU neurons each compute Σwx+b and clamp negative values. They use different connection weights.
explain.dnn.step.2.title: Read out linearly
explain.dnn.step.2.body: The readout weights both hidden activations and adds a bias to form a raw score.
explain.dnn.step.3.title: Read the recommendation score
explain.dnn.step.3.body: Change the candidate to compare hidden activations and final output.
explain.pnn.summary: Add an inner-product feature to the concatenated user/item vectors, then use an MLP.
explain.pnn.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.pnn.difference: Adds an explicit product feature before nonlinear prediction.
explain.pnn.step.0.title: Prepare base features
explain.pnn.step.0.body: Inputs are two-dimensional user and candidate vectors.
explain.pnn.step.1.title: Compute an explicit product feature
explain.pnn.step.1.body: Multiply matching dimensions and sum them to obtain an extra interaction feature.
explain.pnn.step.2.title: Feed features into the MLP
explain.pnn.step.2.body: The original four dimensions and inner-product value enter ReLU hidden neurons and a linear readout together.
explain.pnn.step.3.title: Inspect the interaction score
explain.pnn.step.3.body: Trace output connections left to distinguish the contributions of base features and the product feature.
explain.deepfm.summary: Average a dot-product interaction score and a deep-network score over concatenated vectors.
explain.deepfm.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.deepfm.difference: This implementation combines the FM and deep scores; it has no separate wide linear branch.
explain.deepfm.step.0.title: Share the same inputs
explain.deepfm.step.0.body: User and candidate features feed both a shallow product branch and a deep branch.
explain.deepfm.step.1.title: Compute two branches
explain.deepfm.step.1.body: The FM path sums dimensionwise products; the DNN path uses two ReLU neurons and a linear readout.
explain.deepfm.step.2.title: Average both scores
explain.deepfm.step.2.body: As in this project, the fusion node adds FM and DNN scores and divides by 2.
explain.deepfm.step.3.title: Read the fused result
explain.deepfm.step.3.body: Inspect the output and its sources to compare shallow interactions and nonlinear transformations.
explain.dcn.summary: Build explicit cross features alongside an MLP, then combine them.
explain.dcn.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.dcn.difference: Cross layers repeatedly interact with the original input; the deep branch learns implicit patterns.
explain.dcn.step.0.title: Retain the original x0
explain.dcn.step.0.body: The four concatenated dimensions serve as the Cross base and the DNN input.
explain.dcn.step.1.title: Cross with vector weights
explain.dcn.step.1.body: Compute wᵀx, multiply it by each x0 dimension, and add the residual. A parallel DNN also computes its score.
explain.dcn.step.2.title: Fuse Cross and DNN
explain.dcn.step.2.body: A linear fusion node reads all crossed dimensions and the DNN score.
explain.dcn.step.3.title: Output the interaction score
explain.dcn.step.3.body: Inspect each term of x0×(wᵀx)+x; cross-layer biases are 0 in this example.
explain.dcnv2.summary: Use matrix cross layers or low-rank expert mixtures with the configured deep structure.
explain.dcnv2.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.dcnv2.difference: Supports stacked, parallel and cross-only variants; DCN uses a simpler cross transform.
explain.dcnv2.step.0.title: Read concatenated features
explain.dcnv2.step.0.body: Four input dimensions come from the user and candidate.
explain.dcnv2.step.1.title: Apply a matrix cross and residual
explain.dcnv2.step.1.body: Matrix W produces a different mixture for each dimension, then multiplies by x0 and adds a residual.
explain.dcnv2.step.2.title: Fuse the deep branch
explain.dcnv2.step.2.body: Weight the matrix-cross features and the DNN readout together to form one score.
explain.dcnv2.step.3.title: Inspect matrix effects
explain.dcnv2.step.3.body: Hover over Wx nodes to inspect row weights and compare matrix crossing with ordinary DCN.
explain.autoint.summary: Treat the user and item as feature fields and learn their interactions with self-attention.
explain.autoint.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.autoint.difference: Attention acts on user/item feature fields here, rather than on the user history sequence.
explain.autoint.step.0.title: Treat user and item as fields
explain.autoint.step.0.body: Two fields, each with two dimensions, act as information sources for one another.
explain.autoint.step.1.title: Attend between fields
explain.autoint.step.1.body: Each head projects Q/K/V, then computes between-field scores, softmax, and weighted values.
explain.autoint.step.2.title: Read out interaction features
explain.autoint.step.2.body: Both contextual field features feed a weighted-sum readout.
explain.autoint.step.3.title: Compare candidate effects
explain.autoint.step.3.body: Changing the candidate alters field attention and the final score; inspect nodes to locate the affected calculations.
explain.din.summary: Use each candidate to weight historical items, then score the pooled history with a DNN.
explain.din.difference: Requires unpooled history with masks; this repository supports ranking only. Attention softmax is optional.
explain.din.step.0.title: Keep candidate and history
explain.din.step.0.body: v is the candidate and x1…x3 are history items, retained rather than pre-pooled into a fixed user vector.
explain.din.step.1.title: Compare candidate with each event
explain.din.step.1.body: Differences, products, candidate, and history features feed local activation networks, followed by optional softmax enabled here.
explain.din.step.2.title: Pool a candidate-specific interest
explain.din.step.2.body: Weight history by α and read out a score through a small DNN. Each candidate produces its own history contributions.
explain.din.step.3.title: Read the dynamic interest score
explain.din.step.3.body: Switch candidates to compare local activations, interest vectors, and the green output.
explain.miner.summary: Score each candidate against several user interests, then aggregate the interest scores.
explain.miner.difference: Uses a multi-vector user representation and supports matching only.
explain.miner.step.0.title: Keep two interests
explain.miner.step.0.body: Inputs retain two separate interest vectors and the current candidate.
explain.miner.step.1.title: Match each interest
explain.miner.step.1.body: Each interest multiplies dimensionwise with the candidate to prepare its separate score.
explain.miner.step.2.title: Score and reduce
explain.miner.step.2.body: Sum products into interest scores, then use target-aware attention weighting, max, or mean.
explain.miner.step.3.title: Output one candidate score
explain.miner.step.3.body: The green node is the reduced result. Inspect weighted or reduce nodes for the contributions of both interests.
explain.masknet.summary: Generate feature masks from the input and apply them inside serial or parallel mask blocks.
explain.masknet.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.masknet.difference: Masks modulate feature dimensions for each input instance; these are not sequence-padding masks.
explain.masknet.step.0.title: Read input features
explain.masknet.step.0.body: Four user and candidate dimensions provide content and also generate masks.
explain.masknet.step.1.title: Generate and apply masks
explain.masknet.step.1.body: ReLU mask nodes compute dimensionwise strengths; input features are layer-normalized and multiplied by the masks.
explain.masknet.step.2.title: Pass through one mask block
explain.masknet.step.2.body: Modulated features enter a ReLU projection and a linear readout; one block is expanded here.
explain.masknet.step.3.title: Inspect feature modulation
explain.masknet.step.3.body: Hover over mask and product nodes to compare content values with mask strengths.
explain.gdcn.summary: Gate explicit feature crosses before producing the final prediction.
explain.gdcn.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.gdcn.difference: Adds gates to control cross-feature contributions; topology follows its configured mode.
explain.gdcn.step.0.title: Read inputs and gate sources
explain.gdcn.step.0.body: The same inputs drive the matrix cross, sigmoid gates, and DNN.
explain.gdcn.step.1.title: Gate each crossed dimension
explain.gdcn.step.1.body: Form x0×Wx, multiply by gate, then add the residual. Inspect how sigmoid controls the transmitted fraction.
explain.gdcn.step.2.title: Fuse gated features
explain.gdcn.step.2.body: Gated dimensions and the deep score enter the fusion neuron.
explain.gdcn.step.3.title: Read controlled interactions
explain.gdcn.step.3.body: Trace the effects of matrix mixing, gate values, and residuals separately.
explain.finalmlp.summary: Feed the concatenated vectors into two MLP streams and fuse their outputs with learned interactions.
explain.finalmlp.use: Use for learning or computing user–item relevance scores.
explain.finalmlp.difference: Uses two feature-processing streams and interaction aggregation rather than a single MLP.
explain.finalmlp.step.0.title: Share one input
explain.finalmlp.step.0.body: Four user and candidate dimensions feed two independent MLP streams.
explain.finalmlp.step.1.title: Learn two hidden representations
explain.finalmlp.step.1.body: MLP1 and MLP2 use different weights and ReLU to form two two-dimensional representations.
explain.finalmlp.step.2.title: Fuse bilinear interactions
explain.finalmlp.step.2.body: Multiply every pair across the streams and apply bilinear weights; add a separate linear term to the sum.
explain.finalmlp.step.3.title: Read the two-stream result
explain.finalmlp.step.3.body: Trace the green output back to four interaction terms and the linear term to inspect each contribution.
explain.matching_task.summary: Trains by distinguishing a positive item from sampled negatives.
explain.matching_task.difference: Sets use_neg_sampling=true and uses CrossEntropyLoss; the predictor must support matching.
explain.matching_task.step.0.title: Read candidates and trainable weights
explain.matching_task.step.0.body: The first of three candidates is positive; w is the shared two-dimensional scoring weight.
explain.matching_task.step.1.title: Score and apply softmax
explain.matching_task.step.1.body: Dot each candidate with w to obtain logits, then normalize all three logits into probabilities.
explain.matching_task.step.2.title: Compute positive-example loss
explain.matching_task.step.2.body: CE computes −ln(p1). Inspect the current positive probability and resulting loss.
explain.matching_task.step.3.title: Backpropagate and update
explain.matching_task.step.3.body: Compute ∂L/∂s=p−y, then ∂L/∂w. Update w at learning rate 0.5 and recalculate all three scores and the loss.
explain.ranking_task.summary: Trains each interaction against a binary label using a raw score.
explain.ranking_task.use: Use for pointwise ranking with positive and negative interaction labels.
explain.ranking_task.difference: Sets use_neg_sampling=false and uses BCEWithLogitsLoss. This is pointwise training, not a listwise sorting loss.
explain.ranking_task.step.0.title: Read a click example
explain.ranking_task.step.0.body: One candidate, weights w, bias b, and click label y define this example.
explain.ranking_task.step.1.title: Score and produce probability
explain.ranking_task.step.1.body: Compute z=w·x+b, then sigmoid probability p. Inspect the weighted sum and activation.
explain.ranking_task.step.2.title: Compute binary cross-entropy
explain.ranking_task.step.2.body: BCE uses the logit and label in a numerically stable formula. Change y to compare clicked and unclicked examples.
explain.ranking_task.step.3.title: Update weights and bias
explain.ranking_task.step.3.body: Use p−y to update w and b, then recompute loss. The orange path shows parameters moving toward lower loss.

mechanism.cnn.title: Title token features
mechanism.cnn.singleFeature: This channel of the item vector
mechanism.attention.rows: Each row is a query position; columns are source positions. Rows sum to 1.
mechanism.attention.keepInterests: Both vectors remain available. A sports candidate can use the sports interest, while a cooking candidate can use the cooking interest.
mechanism.attention.projectThenPool: Combine both heads → output projection → additive pooling
mechanism.attention.twoHeads: For this small example, heads are averaged, the output projection is identity, and pooling weights are [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]. Real projections are learned.
mechanism.gru.gateNote: Teaching values: the update gate is 0.5 and h̃ is a chosen candidate activation. A real GRU learns reset/update gates and candidate states from its input and previous state.
mechanism.gru.final: Final state before the output projection
mechanism.gru.compare: Reverse the order and compare the final state. The same three inputs can produce a different representation; the final linear projection is omitted here.
mechanism.pooling.mask: Padding does not add a valid position
mechanism.pooling.compare: Switch the rule: mean reflects the whole sequence, while max keeps the largest value in each dimension. No attention weights are learned.
mechanism.flatten.tokens: Expand content from consecutive history items
mechanism.flatten.difference: Here the model reads content tokens across historical items, rather than one precomputed vector per item. [SEP] denotes a configured item separator.
mechanism.flatten.result: Cross-item token interactions contribute to the final user representation.
mechanism.layers: Look inside the stacked encoder blocks
mechanism.transformer.exchange: Each position first reads other positions, then its features pass through an MLP. Residual paths retain earlier information.
mechanism.transformer.output: After the final block, a linear projection and additive attention compress the valid positions into one vector.
mechanism.transformer.depth: The three blocks are illustrative. The actual number is set by num_hidden_layers.
mechanism.finalPooling: Pool the sequence after contextual encoding
mechanism.fast.global: Replace pairwise comparisons with global summaries
mechanism.fast.output: The Fastformer model pools its contextual states, then the operator projects the result into the recommendation space.
mechanism.lm.context: Compare two uses of the same word
mechanism.lm.cache: Read pooled states from selected LM layers
mechanism.lm.backbone: The backbone builds context-sensitive token states
mechanism.lm.noRepeatedBackbone: The frozen backbone is run to build layer caches. Recommendation training reads the selected caches and trains the side network.
mechanism.lm.bypass: This path skips contextual backbone layers. The vector for “Apple” stays the same across these contexts; other token vectors can differ.
mechanism.lm.contextChange: Change the sentence: the same “Apple” token receives a different contextual state. These are illustrative representations, not a generated continuation.
mechanism.lm.gatedSide: Fuse cached layers through gates and side blocks
mechanism.lm.attention: Project states, then use additive attention
mechanism.lm.san: The shown average is the input to a SAN block. The actual SAN applies a residual MLP and normalization before the next gated fusion.
mechanism.lm.projection: Align the representation with the recommendation model
mechanism.lm.beforeProjection: Pooled vector before final dimension alignment
mechanism.lm.dimensions: W and b align the output dimension. Imported language-model width and recommendation hidden_size can differ.
mechanism.pass.output: The predictor receives the original sequence
mechanism.pass.din: For DIN, the candidate-specific attention is computed later in the predictor. This component preserves the sequence and mask instead of pooling them.
mechanism.pass.sequence: No learned transformation is applied. The L sequence positions are still present in the output.
mechanism.pass.scflatten: SCFlatten enables the framework’s flattened user-side processing mode while the operator itself still returns the single-column embeddings unchanged.
mechanism.predictor.dnn: A small MLP learns nonlinear combinations
mechanism.predictor.pnn: Add an explicit product feature before the MLP
mechanism.predictor.deepfm: Run FM and deep branches in parallel
mechanism.predictor.dcnv2: Use a matrix to mix feature dimensions
mechanism.predictor.autoint: Let the user and item fields attend to each other
mechanism.predictor.din: The candidate changes how history is weighted
mechanism.predictor.miner: Match the candidate against separate interests
mechanism.predictor.masknet: Modulate feature dimensions with an input-guided mask
mechanism.predictor.finalmlp: Two MLP streams meet in a bilinear fusion
mechanism.predictor.toyWeights: The arithmetic uses deliberately small example weights and activations. Actual network widths, projections and learned weights follow the component parameters.
mechanism.predictor.change: Change the candidate and replay to compare its path through the computation. This output is a raw score, not a calibrated probability.
mechanism.cross.config: This example uses one cross layer, zero biases and a simple parallel readout. DCNv2/GDCN can use other configured structures; those choices change the full network topology.
mechanism.autoint.residual: Shown: one head, identity value projection, and a small output projection. The actual attention layers can include residuals, multiple heads and an optional DNN branch.
mechanism.din.softmax: This example enables din_use_softmax to make weights sum to 1. It is optional in this project. The toy DNN here reads only the pooled history, as this implementation does.
mechanism.masknet.blocks: To isolate masking, normalization and block transforms are taken as identity and the toy readout sums the features. Real MaskNet learns serial/parallel mask blocks and their readout.
mechanism.finalmlp.fusion: Shown: illustrative MLP activations, one bilinear head with identity interaction weights, and linear contributions of 0.7 and 0.2. Real fusion learns both linear terms and the bilinear matrix.
mechanism.training.label: Try a different interaction label
mechanism.training.sampleSet: One positive and two sampled negatives
mechanism.training.logitDemo: For clarity, this demonstration takes a gradient step directly on the scores (learning rate 0.5). Real training backpropagates through these scores and updates trainable network parameters.
mechanism.fast.modulation: Shown: global modulation of values with identity value projections. The full Fastformer block also includes learned projections, residuals and feed-forward processing.
mechanism.transformer.arithmetic: One illustrative position: single-head attention, identity attention output projection, zero dropout, FFN first weights diag(0.5, 2), GELU, an identity second map, and LayerNorm scale=1/bias=0 (epsilon omitted in rounded values).
mechanism.lm.ready: Return the projected, pooled item vector
mechanism.lm.builtinProjection: Built-in pretrained operators project each token state to hidden_size before additive pooling. This two-dimensional example takes that projection as identity.
tour.map: Workspace layout; the current area is highlighted
tour.compact: This area is outside the visible workspace at this window size. The layout map shows its location; widen the window to see it.
tour.canvas.title: Your NAML demo is ready
tour.canvas.body: The canvas shows how the recommendation model is assembled. This demo uses CNN to encode news, additive attention to summarize click history, and a dot product to score candidates. Lines connect the components’ inputs and outputs.
tour.canvas.tip: After the tour, click a node to inspect it. Drag empty canvas space to pan, and use the mouse wheel to zoom.
tour.library.title: Find and understand components
tour.library.body: The left library groups datasets, item encoders, user encoders, predictors and training objectives. Search for a component, then drag it onto the canvas to add it or replace a component with the same role.
tour.library.tip: Hover over a component: ⓘ opens its details. The circled question mark opens a concrete, animated explanation where available.
tour.properties.title: Configure the selected component
tour.properties.body: The right panel follows the node selected on the canvas and shows its parameters. When no node is selected, it shows experiment and training settings such as batch size, learning rate and device.
tour.properties.tip: Try selecting the CNN or additive-attention node after the tour. Read a parameter’s description before changing its value.
tour.toolbar.title: Check, generate, then run
tour.toolbar.body: The top toolbar provides save/import/export, templates, undo/redo and theme/language controls. Validate checks the model graph; Generate Model creates its configuration. Train and Evaluate are separate actions that you start yourself.
tour.toolbar.tip: A useful first experiment: replace additive attention with GRU, then validate and generate the model configuration.
tour.results.title: Follow logs and inspect results
tour.results.body: The bottom panel separates validation messages, YAML preview, training progress, evaluation metrics, comparisons and Graph JSON. Use its tabs to inspect each part of a run, and the arrow to collapse or expand the panel.
tour.results.tip: You are ready to explore. If validation reports an error, read its explanation here before starting a run. Reopen the welcome screen and choose Open NAML Demo to see this tour again.
tour.benchmark.title: Benchmark: explore reference results
tour.benchmark.body: Benchmark opens a separate page of published Legommenders experiments. Filter by dataset, search for a model or language model, and sort by GAUC, MRR or NDCG metrics. Results report a mean and standard deviation across runs.
tour.benchmark.tip: Select a result to inspect seed-level metrics, completion status and the run command. After this tour, use Benchmark to explore; Back to Studio returns to your model.
mechanism.flatten.separator: [SEP] is the configured separator between historical items.
neuron.inputSource: This is a given example input. Follow its outgoing connections to inspect how it is used.
neuron.parameterSource: This is an example parameter. The training demonstration updates it using its gradient.
neuron.rounding: Values are shown to 5 decimal places; downstream computations use full precision.
neuron.note.sharedKernel: The three convolution neurons share the same kernel weights.
neuron.note.ceGradient: For softmax with cross-entropy, ∂L/∂s = p−y. The first candidate is the positive example.
neuron.note.weightUpdate: Gradient descent: w′ = w−η·∂L/∂w, with learning rate η = 0.5.
neuron.hint: Hover to trace connections · Click for calculations · Scroll to explore
neuron.inspect: Press Enter for calculations; use arrow keys to move between nodes
neuron.label: Observed click label
neuron.teaching: Circles are scalar neurons or explicitly labeled operation nodes; connections show actual dependencies. Values and weights are teaching examples, not trained model parameters. No real training is run.
neuron.sample.cnn: Inputs x1…x5 are one embedding channel for five title tokens; c1…c3 are responses to three adjacent windows.
neuron.sample.history: x1…x3 are two-dimensional features for reading events; each circle is one dimension. In item encoders they represent token / field features.
neuron.sample.sequence: This example uses two positions with two dimensions each. Regular encoders process tokens or items; Flatten encoders process tokens flattened across history.
neuron.sample.predictor: u is the user feature vector and v is the candidate item vector. Each two-dimensional vector becomes two input circles. Changing the candidate recomputes the network.
neuron.sample.din: v is the candidate; x1…x3 are reading history. Comparing each history item with the candidate produces a candidate-specific interest.
neuron.sample.miner: interest1 and interest2 are two user interest vectors; v is the candidate. Score each interest separately, then reduce to one score.
neuron.sample.lm: token1 represents “chip”; token2 represents context. Switching phone / recipe keeps the initial “chip” vector unchanged, revealing the effect of context.
neuron.sample.iisan: L1…L3 are cached token features from three layers: two tokens with two dimensions each. Changing context replaces these cached inputs.
neuron.sample.training: candidate contains item features; w and b are trainable parameters. Orange nodes show gradients and parameter updates, followed by a new loss calculation.
neuron.example.tiny: A small executable example is expanded here.
neuron.example.cnn: Example: one width-3 convolution channel, ReLU, and learned additive attention pooling.
neuron.example.cnncat: The title branch is expanded and concatenated with an already encoded category vector. CNNCat encodes configured fields separately before concatenation.
neuron.example.ada: Example: tanh scoring, softmax normalization, and a weighted sum.
neuron.example.polyattention: Two context codes compute separate attention distributions, producing two interest vectors.
neuron.example.attention: For inspection, this example uses two positions and two attention heads, with one dimension per head.
neuron.example.gru: This example follows PyTorch GRU reset gates, update gates, and candidate states, then projects the result. Gates depend on both input and previous state.
neuron.example.pooling: All mask values are 1, with no padding. Pooling is a parameter-free operation, not a trainable neuron.
neuron.example.fastformer: This example expands the core global query / key, elementwise modulation, residual, and attention pooling path; surrounding wrapper layers are omitted.
neuron.example.transformer: One two-head block is shown, including residuals, layer normalization, and a GELU feed-forward layer, followed by projection and pooling.
neuron.example.lm: Only a reduced attention sublayer and output aggregation are expanded, not a full pretrained model. BERT attends bidirectionally; built-in autoregressive models use a causal mask.
neuron.example.tokenOnly: The token-only path skips contextual attention; embedding lookups are mean-pooled and projected.
neuron.example.iisan: Starting from cached layer features, this example expands gated fusion and a small SAN: up-projection, ReLU, down-projection, residual, and layer normalization. It does not run a full language model.
neuron.example.passthrough: These circles are copy / arrangement operations, not trainable neurons; feature values stay unchanged. Null branches also retain masks.
neuron.example.matching: Only two scoring weights are updated. The first of three candidates is positive; training uses softmax with cross-entropy and learning rate 0.5.
neuron.example.ranking: One candidate, one click label, and a linear scorer illustrate sigmoid with BCE. Both weights and bias are updated at learning rate 0.5.
neuron.example.dot: The dot product adds no trainable interaction layer; its output is an unnormalized score.
neuron.example.dnn: This example expands two ReLU hidden neurons and one linear output.
neuron.example.pnn: Original features and an inner-product feature feed a small MLP.
neuron.example.deepfm: The example computes inner-product and DNN scores in parallel, then averages them as this project does.
neuron.example.dcn: One vector-weight cross layer and a small parallel DNN branch are expanded before score fusion.
neuron.example.dcnv2: One matrix-weight cross layer is expanded, with residuals and a parallel DNN branch.
neuron.example.gdcn: A sigmoid gate modulates one matrix cross layer dimension by dimension, followed by fusion with a DNN.
neuron.example.autoint: Only two-head attention interactions between the user and item fields, plus a linear readout, are expanded.
neuron.example.din: The local activation network uses candidate, history, difference, and product features. This example enables optional softmax, then aggregates history and scores it.
neuron.example.miner: Two interest vectors are supplied directly to compare target-aware weighting, max, and mean score reduction.
neuron.example.masknet: One input-guided ReLU mask block modulates normalized features before a linear readout.
neuron.example.finalmlp: Two small MLP streams and the bilinear fusion core are expanded; the optional feature selection module is omitted.
explain.organization.title: Neuron organization
explain.organization.layout: Each circle represents one scalar. Columns follow dependencies from left to right; a column need not be a complete network layer.
explain.cnn.organization.0.title: Local connections and shared weights
explain.cnn.organization.0.body: x1…x5 are one feature channel across five tokens. Each of c1…c3 connects to three neighboring inputs; the three ReLU neurons share kernel weights.
explain.cnn.organization.1.title: Attention junction
explain.cnn.organization.1.body: The conv tanh scoring nodes and α nodes form an attention branch. Each α depends on all scores and multiplies its corresponding convolution response.
explain.cnn.organization.2.title: One channel of output
explain.cnn.organization.2.body: The title node sums weighted responses; green out is the output of this channel. A full encoder can use more convolution channels in parallel.
explain.cnncat.organization.0.title: Title convolution branch
explain.cnncat.organization.0.body: x1…x5 feed c1…c3 with shared convolution weights, followed by attention pooling into one title feature.
explain.cnncat.organization.1.title: Separate category branch
explain.cnncat.organization.1.body: category[1] and category[2] are already encoded category dimensions. They bypass title convolution and retain their values on a separate branch.
explain.cnncat.organization.2.title: Concatenation rather than addition
explain.cnncat.organization.2.body: Green nodes retain the title value and two category values as three output dimensions. Fields concatenate at the output and remain separate during pooling.
explain.ada.organization.0.title: Grouped by input
explain.ada.organization.0.body: Two circles per x form a two-dimensional vector. Both dimensions connect to one tanh scoring branch.
explain.ada.organization.1.title: Shared normalization
explain.ada.organization.1.body: All add scores feed the softmax α nodes. The α values are positions in one attention distribution, not separate hidden layers.
explain.ada.organization.2.title: Dimensionwise convergence
explain.ada.organization.2.body: Each input is multiplied by its own α, then matching dimensions converge at pool. Two green outputs form one pooled vector.
explain.attention.organization.0.title: Two positions, two attention heads
explain.attention.organization.0.body: Each position has two input dimensions. attnQ, attnK, and attnV are projection neurons; head indices distinguish two parallel attention branches.
explain.attention.organization.1.title: Interactions within a head
explain.attention.organization.1.body: Within each head, Q connects to K at each position to create scores. Softmax weights V, and head nodes retain contextual results at each position.
explain.attention.organization.2.title: Head merging and pooling
explain.attention.organization.2.body: attnO merges the two heads. The pool scoring and α branch then aggregates positions. Two green circles form one two-dimensional output.
explain.polyattention.organization.0.bod: Three history vectors x pass through a shared tanh projection. Two interest branches connect different context codes to those projected features.
explain.polyattention.organization.1.bod: Each interest has its own scores and α distribution, while both weight the same original history vectors. The branches can attend to different events.
explain.polyattention.organization.2.bod: Each branch converges dimensionwise. Four green circles form two separate two-dimensional interest vectors, retained instead of pooled into one.
explain.gru.organization.0.title: Time positions and inputs
explain.gru.organization.0.body: x1, x2, and x3 are reading events; h0 is the initial state. r1/z1/h1, r2/z2/h2, and r3/z3/h3 belong to three time positions.
explain.gru.organization.1.title: Gated connections inside a cell
explain.gru.organization.1.body: Each r and z receives both the current input and previous state. n is the candidate state; new and keep product branches merge into the next h.
explain.gru.organization.2.title: State chain and output projection
explain.gru.organization.2.body: Each h connects across columns to the next cell, carrying memory. Final h3 projects through Wout into green outputs. Reversing input order changes this state chain.
explain.pooling.organization.0.title: Features and validity nodes
explain.pooling.organization.0.body: Each x has two dimensions and connects to its own mask. valid nodes multiply features by validity flags; all masks are 1 here.
explain.pooling.organization.1.title: Fan-in by dimension
explain.pooling.organization.1.body: Each mean or max node connects to the same dimension across all inputs: records converge while feature dimensions stay aligned.
explain.pooling.organization.2.title: Parameter-free aggregation
explain.pooling.organization.2.body: Two green circles form the pooled vector. Gray circles here are pooling operations, not trainable neurons; switching rules changes the aggregation.
explain.transformer.organization.0.title: Attention sublayer
explain.transformer.organization.0.body: Two positions each have two input dimensions. T Q/K/V, score, softmax, and head nodes form two parallel attention heads, merged by O projections.
explain.transformer.organization.1.title: Residual and feed-forward sublayers
explain.transformer.organization.1.body: r1 adds input and attention output before LN1. FF and W2 form the feed-forward network; r2 and LN2 provide the second residual and normalization.
explain.transformer.organization.2.title: Position aggregation
explain.transformer.organization.2.body: Each position projects through P into the pool attention branch, which converges into two green output dimensions. One reduced encoder block is expanded.
explain.fastformer.organization.0.title: Global query branch
explain.fastformer.organization.0.body: Each position connects to Q and K projections. Q scores and α converge at q̄, a global query shared across positions.
explain.fastformer.organization.1.title: Global key and modulation
explain.fastformer.organization.1.body: q̄ fans out to multiply each K; the β branch converges into k̄. This global key connects to each content dimension for elementwise modulation.
explain.fastformer.organization.2.title: Residual, pooling, and output
explain.fastformer.organization.2.body: res nodes reconnect Q, pool aggregates positions, and Wout projects into green outputs. The graph expands the global-attention core path.
explain.lm.organization.0.title: Token positions and context
explain.lm.organization.0.body: token1 is “chip” and token2 is context, with two circles per position. LMQ/K/V represent projections in an attention sublayer.
explain.lm.organization.1.title: Attention dependency range
explain.lm.organization.1.body: Two head branches compute position interactions separately. The BERT example has bidirectional connections; autoregressive examples connect only to current and earlier positions.
explain.lm.organization.2.title: Projection and aggregation exit
explain.lm.organization.2.body: Contextual positions project through W and converge through pool into green outputs. This is a reduced attention core, not the full pretrained model.
explain.iisan.organization.0.title: Parallel cached-layer inputs
explain.iisan.organization.0.body: L1…L3 are cached token features from different layers. cacheL nodes first average tokens by dimension into three layer representations.
explain.iisan.organization.1.title: Gated fusion and SAN cells
explain.iisan.organization.1.body: μ and 1−μ weight the old state and next layer; fuse merges them. SANup, SANdown, SANres, and SANnorm form the up/down-projection, residual, and normalization cell.
explain.iisan.organization.2.title: Adapters chained across layers
explain.iisan.organization.2.body: Each SAN output enters the next fusion, followed by Wout and green item features. Cached layers are given inputs; the language model is not rerun in the graph.
explain.externalhf.organization.0.title: Two encoding paths
explain.externalhf.organization.0.body: token1 and token2 are word positions. Contextual mode includes LMQ/K/V and attention branches; token-only mode uses lookup nodes for embedding lookups.
explain.externalhf.organization.1.title: Cross-token connections
explain.externalhf.organization.1.body: In contextual mode, a position can receive information from another. In token-only mode, words stay independent until pooling.
explain.externalhf.organization.2.title: Shared output structure
explain.externalhf.organization.2.body: Both paths converge dimensionwise at mean pooling, then project through Wout into two green outputs. The attention sublayer is a reduced teaching example.
explain.dot.organization.0.title: Two groups of input dimensions
explain.dot.organization.0.body: u[1] and u[2] belong to the user; v[1] and v[2] to the candidate item. A circle is one vector dimension, not an entire user or item.
explain.dot.organization.1.title: Paired connections
explain.dot.organization.1.body: Each of two product nodes receives matching dimensions of u and v. There is no fully connected hidden layer.
explain.dot.organization.2.title: One sum exit
explain.dot.organization.2.body: Both products converge at u·v and pass into green score. This is a raw relevance score without probability normalization.
explain.dnn.organization.0.title: Four concatenated inputs
explain.dnn.organization.0.body: u and v each occupy two circles, forming four input dimensions for the hidden layer.
explain.dnn.organization.1.title: Fully connected hidden layer
explain.dnn.organization.1.body: MLPh1 and MLPh2 each connect to all four inputs, using separate weights and biases followed by ReLU.
explain.dnn.organization.2.title: Linear readout
explain.dnn.organization.2.body: MLPz merges both hidden neurons; green score retains its value. This small network exposes the input, hidden, and readout organization.
explain.pnn.organization.0.title: Original-feature path
explain.pnn.organization.0.body: All four dimensions of u and v connect directly to the later PNN hidden neurons, retaining original features.
explain.pnn.organization.1.title: Additional product branch
explain.pnn.organization.1.body: Matching dimensions feed product nodes, then converge at u·v. This interaction value becomes a fifth hidden-layer input alongside the original four.
explain.pnn.organization.2.title: Hidden layer and readout
explain.pnn.organization.2.body: PNNh1 and PNNh2 are ReLU neurons, merged by PNNz into a green score. The product branch supplies an explicit interaction feature.
explain.deepfm.organization.0.title: Two branches sharing inputs
explain.deepfm.organization.0.body: The same u and v inputs fan out into FM and DNN paths, which use user and candidate features in parallel.
explain.deepfm.organization.1.title: Shallow interactions and deep transforms
explain.deepfm.organization.1.body: FM consists of matching-dimension products and a sum. DNN contains two ReLU hidden neurons and a linear readout.
explain.deepfm.organization.2.title: Averaged output junction
explain.deepfm.organization.2.body: Both scores connect to average and then green score. Averaging matches this project’s fusion implementation.
explain.dcn.organization.0.title: Inputs shared by two branches
explain.dcn.organization.0.body: The four-dimensional concatenated x0 feeds both Cross and DNN. Long connections preserve direct dependencies on the original input.
explain.dcn.organization.1.title: Vector-weight cross layer
explain.dcn.organization.1.body: crossScale nodes use the same vector weights to compute wᵀx. Each x0 dimension multiplies this quantity and merges with its own residual at x1.
explain.dcn.organization.2.title: Cross and deep feature junction
explain.dcn.organization.2.body: fusion connects all x1 dimensions and the DNN readout into one green score. One Cross layer is expanded.
explain.dcnv2.organization.0.title: Parallel Cross and DNN
explain.dcnv2.organization.0.body: Four input dimensions feed both the matrix cross network and the deep branch.
explain.dcnv2.organization.1.title: Matrix-weight dimensionwise cross
explain.dcnv2.organization.1.body: Each Wx node uses a different matrix row to produce a dimension-specific mixture. cross multiplies it by x0; x1 reconnects the residual.
explain.dcnv2.organization.2.title: Fusion into one exit
explain.dcnv2.organization.2.body: All x1 dimensions and the DNN score connect to fusion and then green score. One matrix Cross layer is expanded.
explain.gdcn.organization.0.title: Cross, gate, and deep branches
explain.gdcn.organization.0.body: The same inputs fan out to Wx, gate, and DNN, providing interaction content, transmission fractions, and deep features.
explain.gdcn.organization.1.title: Gating each dimension
explain.gdcn.organization.1.body: cross forms x0×Wx. Each sigmoid gate connects to its matching gated product, and x1 reconnects the input residual.
explain.gdcn.organization.2.title: Unified readout
explain.gdcn.organization.2.body: fusion merges gated dimensions with the DNN readout; green score outputs one candidate score. One gated Cross layer is shown.
explain.autoint.organization.0.title: Fields rather than time positions
explain.autoint.organization.0.body: u and v are user and candidate fields, each with two input dimensions. fieldQ/K/V are projections for field attention.
explain.autoint.organization.1.title: Two-head field interactions
explain.autoint.organization.1.body: Each head lets both fields connect to each other, using scores, softmax, and weighted V to create contextual field features.
explain.autoint.organization.2.title: Field readout junction
explain.autoint.organization.2.body: fieldO merges heads; readout consumes all dimensions from both fields and produces a green score. The graph expands the attention-interaction core.
explain.din.organization.0.title: Shared candidate, separate history branches
explain.din.organization.0.body: v fans out into three DIN branches; each history x enters its own comparison branch. A different candidate changes these branch inputs.
explain.din.organization.1.title: Local activation networks
explain.din.organization.1.body: Each branch connects v, x, their difference, and dimensionwise products to a small ReLU network that produces an attention score. Optional softmax is enabled here to obtain α.
explain.din.organization.2.title: Candidate-specific interest exit
explain.din.organization.2.body: α reconnects to original history and converges by dimension at interest; the final DNN outputs a score. The current candidate determines the pooled interest.
explain.miner.organization.0.title: Two separate interest groups
explain.miner.organization.0.body: interest1 and interest2 each have two dimensions and connect to the same candidate v. Interests are given inputs; their upstream encoder is not expanded.
explain.miner.organization.1.title: Two independent scoring branches
explain.miner.organization.1.body: Each interest multiplies matching dimensions with v, converging separately at interestScore1 and interestScore2 without mixing interests early.
explain.miner.organization.2.title: Selectable score junction
explain.miner.organization.2.body: Target-aware mode adds projection, attention, and weighted branches. Max or mean mode uses reduce to merge both scores directly. The green exit is always a single score.
explain.masknet.organization.0.title: Content and mask branches
explain.masknet.organization.0.body: Four inputs feed both norm normalization and mask ReLU projections. The current input determines the masks.
explain.masknet.organization.1.title: One-to-one modulation
explain.masknet.organization.1.body: Each normalized dimension multiplies only its matching mask at mask×h. Masks change feature strength rather than remove entire records.
explain.masknet.organization.2.title: One block and its readout
explain.masknet.organization.2.body: All four modulated dimensions connect to two block neurons, followed by readout and a green score. One Mask block is expanded.
explain.finalmlp.organization.0.title: Two independent MLP streams
explain.finalmlp.organization.0.body: The same u and v connect to MLP1 and MLP2. Separate weights produce two different two-dimensional hidden representations.
explain.finalmlp.organization.1.title: Pairwise connections across streams
explain.finalmlp.organization.1.body: Each MLP1 dimension multiplies each MLP2 dimension, creating four h1h2 interaction terms; B nodes apply bilinear weights.
explain.finalmlp.organization.2.title: Linear and bilinear junction
explain.finalmlp.organization.2.body: linear reads both hidden representations directly. fusion adds that linear term and four interaction terms, connecting to green score.
explain.matching_task.organization.0.bod: Three candidates each have two dimensions and share purple w parameters. Separate s scores connect to the same softmax probability distribution p.
explain.matching_task.organization.1.bod: CE connects to positive probability p1. Orange ∂L/∂s nodes use p−y, then candidate features converge into shared-weight gradients ∂L/∂w.
explain.matching_task.organization.2.bod: w′ holds updated parameters; s′, p′, and CE′ rescore and recompute loss with them. The orange path represents differentiation and updates, not another hidden layer.
explain.ranking_task.organization.0.body: candidate is a two-dimensional item feature; purple w and b are shared parameters, and y is the click label. z combines weighted features and bias; p is sigmoid output.
explain.ranking_task.organization.1.body: BCE connects to both z and y. The orange p−y branch produces ∂L/∂z and supplies gradients for each w dimension and b.
explain.ranking_task.organization.2.body: w′ and b′ connect to new score z′. BCE′ and original BCE compare loss before and after the update. Gradients also expand rightward by dependency for inspection.
Input positions are tokens flattened across reading history, rather than one node per item. Q/K/V attention heads operate on these token positions.
r1 adds input and attention output before LN1. FF and W2 form the feed-forward network; r2 and LN2 provide the second residual and normalization.
Each position projects through P into the pool attention branch, which converges into two green output dimensions. One reduced encoder block is expanded.
explain.flattenfastformer.organization.0: Inputs are tokens flattened across reading history. Token Q scores and α converge at q̄, a global query shared by the flattened sequence.
explain.flattenfastformer.organization.1: q̄ fans out to multiply each K; the β branch converges into k̄. This global key connects to each content dimension for elementwise modulation.
explain.flattenfastformer.organization.2: res nodes reconnect Q, pool aggregates positions, and Wout projects into green outputs. The graph expands the global-attention core path.
explain.nullsimple.organization.0.title: Retained input structure
explain.nullsimple.organization.0.body: Inputs retain history items, each x represented by two dimensions.
explain.nullsimple.organization.1.title: One-to-one copy connections
explain.nullsimple.organization.1.body: Each input connects only to its own copy and pass nodes, with weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trainable hidden layers.
explain.nullsimple.organization.2.title: Outputs without aggregation
explain.nullsimple.organization.2.body: Each original dimension maps to a separate green output, without pooling or attention. Trailing maskCopy branches retain validity flags.
explain.nullconcat.organization.0.title: Retained input structure
explain.nullconcat.organization.0.body: Inputs represent concatenated history features, displayed as retained dimensions grouped by x.
explain.nullconcat.organization.1.title: One-to-one copy connections
explain.nullconcat.organization.1.body: Each input connects only to its own copy and pass nodes, with weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trainable hidden layers.
explain.nullconcat.organization.2.title: Outputs without aggregation
explain.nullconcat.organization.2.body: Each original dimension maps to a separate green output, without pooling or attention. Trailing maskCopy branches retain validity flags.
explain.scsimple.organization.0.title: Retained input structure
explain.scsimple.organization.0.body: Inputs come from a single feature column, with two example dimensions retained for each x.
explain.scsimple.organization.1.title: One-to-one copy connections
explain.scsimple.organization.1.body: Each input connects only to its own copy and pass nodes, with weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trainable hidden layers.
explain.scsimple.organization.2.title: Outputs without aggregation
explain.scsimple.organization.2.body: Each original dimension maps to a separate green output, without pooling or attention. Variants differ in input granularity and organization.
explain.scflatten.organization.0.title: Retained input structure
explain.scflatten.organization.0.body: Inputs are a token sequence flattened from a single column; x dimensions retain token features.
explain.scflatten.organization.1.title: One-to-one copy connections
explain.scflatten.organization.1.body: Each input connects only to its own copy and pass nodes, with weight 1 and bias 0. These are arrangement operations, not new trainable hidden layers.
explain.scflatten.organization.2.title: Outputs without aggregation
explain.scflatten.organization.2.body: Each original dimension maps to a separate green output, without pooling or attention. Variants differ in input granularity and organization.
explain.organization.hint: Hover to highlight · Click to locate. Hover over a neuron to find its explanation.
